prompt: You switch a high-traffic Postgres service to `SERIALIZABLE` (SSI). What new behaviour must the application handle?

options.text: Reads now block writes, so latency rises under load
options.explanation: Wrong. SSI keeps MVCC's non-blocking reads; its SIREAD markers record what was read without blocking anyone. That's what distinguishes it from 2PL.

options.text: Transactions can fail with serialization errors (SQLSTATE 40001) at any statement or at commit, and must be retried
options.explanation: Correct. SSI is optimistic: it lets transactions run and aborts one when it detects a dangerous pattern of read/write dependencies. The app needs a retry loop, and transactions should be short and free of external side effects.

Wrong. Serialization failures are a behavioral change and their frequency and performance cost depend on the workload. Applications need bounded full-transaction retries or an explicit failure response.
Wrong. Rows written still take locks, so deadlocks between writers are still possible. Serialization failures are an *additional* failure mode.

workedExample:
1. SSI tracks dependencies between reads and writes in addition to using snapshots.
2. A dangerous dependency pattern can trigger SQLSTATE 40001 during a statement or at commit.
3. Roll back the entire failed transaction, then retry its complete logic in a new transaction and snapshot with bounded backoff.
Python control-flow fragment: place this inside a request handler. The transaction, rollback and backoff helpers are supplied by the application.
```python
# Retry all logic in a fresh
# transaction.
for attempt in range(1, 6):
  try:
    run_complete_transaction()
    return success
  except SerializationFailure:
    rollback_if_needed()
    # Exhaustion must remain a failure.
    if attempt == 5: raise
    sleep(backoff(attempt))
```
4. Keep nontransactional side effects out of retried transaction bodies. A transactional outbox plus an idempotent downstream protocol closes crash and duplicate windows better than a bare post-commit call.

link.title: Ports and Grittner: Serializable Snapshot Isolation in PostgreSQL

prompt: A team migrating from Oracle to Postgres says: "We ran everything at `SERIALIZABLE` on Oracle, so our booking code was race-free." Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Oracle's Serializable is snapshot isolation, so write skew (such as the on-call doctors bug) could still have happened
options.explanation: Correct. Oracle detects write-write conflicts on the same row (`ORA-08177`) but doesn't track read dependencies, so two transactions writing different rows on the basis of the same read can both commit.

options.text: Oracle offers only Read Committed and Serializable (plus Read Only); it has no Repeatable Read level
options.explanation: Correct. Oracle's default is Read Committed, and its only stronger level is Serializable. Asking it for Repeatable Read isn't an option.

options.text: Postgres Serializable is also snapshot isolation, so nothing changes after the migration
options.explanation: Wrong. Postgres Serializable is SSI: it adds read-dependency tracking on top of snapshots and aborts transactions that could produce write skew. It is genuinely serializable.

options.text: Oracle's Serializable takes shared read locks, which is why it was slow
options.explanation: Wrong. Oracle uses multiversion reads at every level; readers don't take shared locks. That's why its Serializable is snapshot isolation rather than 2PL.

options.text: After moving to Postgres Serializable, the code needs to retry on SQLSTATE 40001
options.explanation: Correct. SSI is optimistic and aborts one transaction of a dangerous pair. Without a retry loop, those aborts become user-facing errors.

workedExample:
Ask what each engine's "Serializable" actually is.

| Engine | Serializable is | Write skew? |
|---|---|---|
| Oracle | Snapshot isolation | Possible |
| Postgres | SSI | Prevented |

1. Oracle: snapshot reads plus first-committer-wins on rows both transactions *wrote*. The doctors case writes different rows, so both commit. (1) true.
2. Oracle's isolation levels are Read Committed (default) and Serializable; READ ONLY is a separate transaction mode. (2) true.
3. Postgres Serializable is SSI, which is stronger, not the same. (3) false.
4. Ordinary Oracle consistent reads do not take shared row locks; explicit locking queries are different. (4) false.
5. SSI aborts with 40001, so retries are required. (5) true.

So the team's code may have had latent write-skew bugs on Oracle that Postgres will now surface as serialization failures.
